reason: ψυχή has several senses, and most of the variation in the run is appropriate sense-splitting (life, soul, person). But the run is inconsistent where 'life' and 'soul' compete. It departs to 'life' at Matt 16:26, Mark 8:36-37, 2 Cor 12:15 and 1 Pet 4:19, yet keeps 'soul' in comparable contexts at Jas 1:21, Jas 5:20, 1 Pet 1:9, 1 Pet 2:25, Heb 10:39 and Heb 13:17. Luke 12:19-20 has 'soul' while 12:22-23 has 'life'. ἐκ ψυχῆς is 'wholeheartedly' at Eph 6:6 but 'with your whole being' at Col 3:23. Acts 14:2 has 'souls' where Acts 15:24 has 'minds'. A register entry is needed to fix the boundaries.
sense: A person's life, as what is saved, lost, found, sought, risked, given, laid down or worried over; this includes the Gospel sayings about saving and losing one's ψυχή. The alternates cover the word's other senses: inner self or soul, individual person, and living creature.

alternates.when: The inner self as seat of feeling, desire, devotion or delight, including God's (Matt 11:29; 12:18; 22:37; 26:38; Mark 12:30; 14:34; Luke 1:46; 2:35; 10:27; John 12:27; Acts 14:22; Heb 10:38; 12:3; 2 Pet 2:8, 14; 3 John 2; Rev 18:14). The ψυχή set against the body as what killing cannot reach, or listed beside spirit (Matt 10:28; 1 Thess 5:23; Heb 4:12). The dead (Acts 2:27; Rev 6:9; 20:4). Unity phrases (Acts 4:32; Phil 1:27). The rich man's self-address and God's reply to it (Luke 12:19-20). In the letters, the ψυχή as object of spiritual care, purification, safekeeping with God or final salvation (2 Cor 12:15; Heb 6:19; 10:39; 13:17; Jas 1:21; 5:20; 1 Pet 1:9, 22; 2:11, 25; 4:19).
The Septuagint idiom in which ψυχή counts or designates individuals: with numbers, or with 'every' (Acts 2:41, 43; 3:23; 7:14; 27:37; Rom 2:9; 13:1; 1 Pet 3:20).
ψυχὴ ζῶσα or ψυχὴ ζωῆς, echoing Genesis, for an animate creature (1 Cor 15:45; Rev 16:3).
The ψυχή as the seat of attitude or conviction that outsiders stir up or unsettle (Acts 14:2; 15:24).
The adverbial phrase ἐκ ψυχῆς (Eph 6:6; Col 3:23).
The idiom τὴν ψυχὴν αἴρειν at John 10:24.

traditional: soul, with life where physical life is plainly meant
rationale: In first-century usage ψυχή most often means a person's life or living self, not an immaterial part of them, so 'life' is the default wherever it is saved, lost, risked or given. That includes Matt 16:26 and Mark 8:36-37, where the argument depends on the word being the same as in the preceding verse. 'Soul' is kept where English still uses it naturally and without misleading: for the inner self that grieves, rejoices and loves, for the ψυχή contrasted with the body or surviving death, and in the letters' language of saving, guarding and shepherding souls. In that last group 'life' would wrongly suggest mere physical rescue.
standard_view: All major translations split the word between 'life', 'soul' and 'person' by context; the disagreement is over where the lines fall. KJV, ESV and NIV have 'soul' at Matt 16:26 and Mark 8:36-37, while NRSV and some others have 'life'. In the letters ('salvation of your souls', 'save your souls') most versions keep 'soul', though many scholars hold that the whole person is meant, and some versions paraphrase as 'you' or 'yourselves' (2 Cor 12:15; 1 Pet 4:19; Heb 10:39). At Luke 12:20 ESV keeps 'soul' while NRSV and NIV have 'life'. At Phil 1:27 many versions have 'one mind'.
